newsitem.title: USA: Tele-Communications to lay off 2,500 employees.
newsitem.headline: Tele-Communications to lay off 2,500 employees.

text.p: Tele-Communications Inc., the nation's largest cable television operator, said Thursday it will cut 2,500 employees, or 6.5 percent of its work force, as it seeks to lower costs and reduce debt.

The Englewood, Colo.-based company also said it would review all expenses not directly related to serving customers and would cut or freeze salaries of senior executives unless it meets business objectives.
TCI faces daunting challenges, including stiff competition from direct broadcast satellite television services whose popularity has been growing faster than experts had expected.
The layoffs, which will come from corporate headquarters and field offices, mean the current work force of 38,500 will be reduced to 36,000, a company spokesman said.

Industry analysts estimated the cuts could save TCI as much as $100 million. TCI said it will take a one-time charge in the current quarter for the cuts but officials declined to specify how big the charge will be.

Workers, who were told Wednesday they would no longer have jobs, will vacate their offices on Friday. Gone also will be the company's fleet of four aircraft, used to fly executives to the many rural areas where TCI has operations.
The announcement followed a meeting this week that Chief Executive John Malone held with a group of investors at the company's headquarters.
The cutbacks come as TCI is looking for ways to reduce debt, improve its lagging financial performance and shore up its stock price after several quarters of disappointing earnings.
Analysts said the cuts also show Malone will be playing a stronger role at TCI.
"He is reasserting himself at the helm," said Ted Henderson, managing director of research at Janco Partners.
Henderson said he viewed the changing world of telecommunications as a horse race with many good horses. "In that case you bet on the jockey and I like Malone."
TCI was also expected to cut programming costs, one of the biggest expenses for the cable operator.
"Programmers better not think they can be content," said A.G. Edwards analyst James Jungjohann.
TCI spokesman Bob Thomson said the cable operator would review its programming to determine what viewers want to see, a move that could result in some stations being dropped.
"We will be doing research, using common sense and gut extinct," he said.
Some channels whose carriage could be scaled back are VH1, the music channel, the Comedy Channel and WGN, the Chicago-based superstation owned by the Tribune Co., Thomson said.
Channels likely to be carried on more TCI systems are Animal Planet, an education station designed by the Discover Channel, the Cartoon Network and House & Garden, he said.
Savings on programming will have a direct impact on cash flow, Janco Partners' Henderson said.
TCI has taken several steps to reap the benefit of smaller operations and has spun off its satellite unit, TCI Satellite Entertainment Inc.
Having a sleeker operation also makes it easier for investors to evaluate the company, Henderson said.
Earlier this year, TCI notified suppliers that it would be cutting back orders to better control inventories.
The company's stock, which has lingered near its 52-week low of $11.25, rose 50 cents to close at $13.625 on Nasdaq.
